extracted.intended_audience: small business owners and representatives preparing public comment letters on federal rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for small businesses on drafting effective public comment letters to federal agencies during notice-and-comment rulemaking, including structure, evidence, tone, and submission timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the proposed regulation in the Federal Register or from the relevant agency and pay attention to the purpose of the regulation and how it might affect your business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully read the proposed rule; identify key points and focus on areas where the regulation could have the most significant impact on your business. (From: 'Review the Proposed Rule' and 'Identify Key Issues'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: State your purpose early
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first few sentences, clearly state that you are submitting a comment letter on a proposed rule and briefly explain why this is important to your business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your purpose explicit at the start so the agency immediately understands who you are and why your comment matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jargon or overly technical language; aim to communicate points clearly and concisely so the regulatory agency can easily understand your concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in plain English; simplify complex phrasing and avoid unnecessary technical terms that may obscure the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the impact on your business (be specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Share concrete examples of how the proposed rule will affect your day-to-day operations (e.g., increases costs, limits growth, creates unnecessary burdens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide real-world examples and detailed descriptions so regulators can visualize the effect. Specificity improves persuasiveness and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide data to support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Include data or evidence where possible, such as cost estimates, operational impacts, or industry benchmarks to support your assertions about the rule's effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When available, quantify impacts (e.g., estimated costs, time burdens). Cite the origin of data. If proprietary concerns exist, give as much non-confidential detail as possible so the agency understands the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer constructive solutions or alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed regulation could be improved, suggest specific changes or alternatives that would allow businesses to comply without significant challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be practical and constructive — propose feasible modifications, highlight how changes could benefit businesses and consumers, and provide examples such as altering a section, delaying compliance dates, or exempting a subset of industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a professional and respectful tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a respectful and constructive tone; avoid emotional language, accusations, anger, sarcasm, or overly complicated phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A professional tone increases credibility and receptiveness. Plain, accessible language is preferred; avoid sarcasm and emotional appeals that detract from substantive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the agency's submission instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comply with each agency's specific instructions for submitting comment letters (formatting, submission process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check agency notices for required formats, methods of filing, and any special procedural requirements to ensure your comment is accepted and considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit within the comment period and as early as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and meet the public comment deadline (often 30 to 60 days); timely submission allows agencies more time to consider feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the comment period on the Federal Register or agency notice and submit before the deadline; early submission can increase the chance your input influences drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a clear introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction should specify who you are, the name of the rule you are commenting on, a brief overview of your business and/or experience relevant to the rule, and a summary paragraph describing the parts of the rule you are concerned about and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the introduction to establish standing and relevance; briefly preview the main points so reviewers know what to expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe support or opposition with explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a section that describes the parts of the rule you support or oppose, with explanations as to why each provision helps or hurts your small business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific and offer supporting data. If you cannot disclose proprietary information, provide sufficient non-confidential information for the agency to understand your argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a brief conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize your main points in about a sentence or two each and thank the agency for considering your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise conclusion reinforces your key recommendations and leaves a professional final impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure arguments beginning with a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Each section should start with a clear claim that contains your main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the claim at the top of a section so reviewers immediately see your position before the supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with specific data types
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide data such as agency assumptions on overall costs, compliance costs for equipment or staff, costs/time to file new paperwork, and other quantifiable impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider agency-cost assumptions, per-provision costs, compliance burdens (equipment, labor), filing burdens (time/cost to complete forms), and revenue impacts. Use numbers or estimates when possible and identify sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address and rebut agency cost-benefit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer an argument why an alternative is better, or respond to an agency's claim that a provision serves as a cost benefit and will not result in cost impacts on your business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how agency estimates may over- or under-state impacts. Explain why your data indicates a different outcome and tie that back to the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why evidence matters (tie claim and data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly connect the data to your claim by explaining how the evidence demonstrates that the rule is burdensome or how an alternative lessens harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the causal link between the regulation and the impact on your business. Provide reasoning that translates numbers into concrete burdens or benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer concrete mitigation options
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose specific mitigations such as altering a section of the rule, delaying the compliance date, or excluding a part of the industry from a requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present feasible, targeted fixes that preserve regulatory goals while reducing undue burden on small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific (general recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more specific information you provide, the better; agencies are more likely to listen to arguments that call on specific data and real-world examples full of details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague statements. Detailed examples and numbers make it easier for regulators to understand and act on your concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite your sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When you provide data and documentation, make very clear where they come from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide citations, links, or references for studies, industry data, or internal estimates so the agency can verify and rely on the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolster your credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain your relevant experience and why the agency should listen to you; be careful not to overstate or inflate estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State your qualifications, relevant expertise, years in business, or operational scope. Honest, well-supported claims increase persuasiveness; exaggeration undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind tone and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid angry tone or sarcasm, but also avoid making your letter too complicated; aim for a clear and accessible tone that lays out the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a balance between professional firmness and plain language; complicated legal or technical prose may reduce accessibility to rule writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread and seek review
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the letter for grammar, spelling, and clarity; ideally have someone trusted review it for errors and unclear arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer isn't available, give yourself time and distance before editing or read the letter aloud to catch issues.
